questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.155: at or above 10,000 ft MSL (and more than 1,200 ft AGL), 5 SM visibility and 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontal from clouds.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What do you need before entering Class B airspace?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.131: you need an ATC clearance, such as “cleared into the Class Bravo airspace”. Radio contact alone isn’t enough.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What do you need before entering Class C airspace?
options: Two-way radio communication established with ATC
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.130: two-way radio communication must be established. If the controller replies using your callsign, communication is established.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What are the typical dimensions of Class C airspace?
options: A 5 NM core from the surface to 4,000 ft AGL, and a shelf out to 10 NM from 1,200 to 4,000 ft AGL
A 30 NM ring up to 10,000 ft MSL
A 4 NM ring up to 2,500 ft AGL
A 10 NM core from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL
questions.explain: Class C is usually a 5 NM radius core from the surface to 4,000 ft above the airport, with a 10 NM shelf from 1,200 ft to 4,000 ft above the airport.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: Where is the “Mode C veil”?
options: Within 10 NM of any towered airport
Within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL
questions.explain: Within 30 NM of the primary airport of Class B airspace, from the surface up to 10,000 ft MSL, you need an altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: At what altitude does Class A airspace begin?
questions.explain: Class A runs from 18,000 ft MSL up to and including FL 600, and requires IFR.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: You’re VFR more than 3,000 ft AGL on a magnetic course of 090°. Which altitude is appropriate?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.159: on magnetic courses 0–179°, fly odd thousands plus 500 ft (such as 3,500 or 5,500). On 180–359°, even thousands plus 500 ft.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What are the special VFR minimums?
options: 1 SM flight visibility, clear of clouds
Half a mile, clear of clouds
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.157: special VFR requires 1 SM flight visibility and remaining clear of clouds. At night it also requires an instrument rating and an IFR-equipped aircraft.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: When may you fly through an active restricted area?
options: Only with permission of the controlling agency
questions.explain: Restricted areas contain hazards such as artillery firing. When active, you need permission from the controlling or using agency.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What should a VFR pilot do in an active Military Operations Area (MOA)?
options: VFR flight is allowed, but be extremely cautious and check with the controlling agency for activity
questions.explain: MOAs separate military training from IFR traffic. VFR flight is permitted, but pilots should exercise extreme caution while military activity is going on.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: On a sectional chart, how is Class D airspace shown?
questions.explain: Class D is a dashed blue line. Class B is solid blue, Class C solid magenta, and Class E to the surface is dashed magenta.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: Which transponder code is used for VFR flight in the US?
questions.explain: VFR aircraft squawk 1200 unless ATC assigns another code. 7000 is the VFR code in much of Europe.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: Where is ADS-B Out required?
options: In Class A, B and C, inside the Mode C veil, and above 10,000 ft MSL (except below 2,500 ft AGL)
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.225 sets the ADS-B Out rule areas, broadly the same places a Mode C transponder is needed.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: In Class G by day, above 1,200 ft AGL but below 10,000 ft MSL, what are the VFR minimums?
options: 1 SM, 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.155: 1 SM visibility by day, and 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal from clouds.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: At a runway holding position marking (two solid and two dashed yellow lines), where do you stop?
questions.explain: Hold on the side with the solid lines. You may cross from the dashed side to leave the runway.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: Runway 27 is aligned closest to which heading?
questions.explain: Runway numbers are the magnetic direction rounded to the nearest 10°, with the last zero dropped.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: A rotating beacon flashes white and green. What does it mark?
questions.explain: White and green is a lighted land airport. White and yellow is a water airport, and green, yellow and white is a heliport.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: The rotating beacon is on during the day at an airport in controlled airspace. What might it mean?
options: The weather may be below VFR minimums (ceiling under 1,000 ft or visibility under 3 SM)
questions.explain: Daytime operation of the beacon in Class B, C, D or E surface areas often means the ceiling is below 1,000 ft and/or visibility below 3 SM. Don’t rely on it; check the weather.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: On a two-bar VASI, what do you see when you’re on the glide path?
questions.explain: “Red over white, you’re all right.” Red over red is low, white over white is high.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: On a four-light PAPI, what shows you’re on the glide path?
questions.explain: Two white and two red is on the glide path. More white is high, more red is low.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: How may you use the runway before a displaced threshold?
options: For taxiing, takeoff, and landing rollout, but not for touchdown
questions.explain: The area before a displaced threshold (marked with white arrows) can be used for taxi, takeoff and the rollout from the opposite direction, but not for landing touchdown.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: An area before the runway is marked with yellow chevrons. How may you use it?
options: Not for taxi, takeoff or landing
questions.explain: Yellow chevrons mark a blast pad or stopway. It isn’t usable for taxi, takeoff or landing.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: Unless shown otherwise, which way are turns in the traffic pattern?
questions.explain: Standard traffic patterns use left turns unless markings, the chart supplement or ATC say otherwise.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: At a nontowered airport, what is the recommended way to enter the traffic pattern?
options: At a 45° angle to the downwind leg, at pattern altitude
Directly over the runway at 500 ft
From the upwind leg above pattern altitude
questions.explain: The AIM recommends entering at a 45° angle to the downwind leg, abeam the midpoint of the runway, at pattern altitude.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: Inbound to a nontowered airport, when does the AIM recommend your first CTAF call?
questions.explain: Make your first call about 10 miles out, then report on downwind, base and final, and when leaving the runway.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What does a sign with a yellow background and black letters and an arrow tell you?
options: A direction to a taxiway or runway
questions.explain: Direction signs are black on yellow with arrows. Location signs (black background, yellow letters) show where you are, and mandatory signs are white on red.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What does a red sign with white letters mean?
options: A mandatory instruction, such as a runway holding position
questions.explain: Red with white letters is a mandatory instruction sign, such as a runway holding position or no-entry area.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Wind directions in a METAR or TAF are referenced to…
questions.explain: Written reports and forecasts (METAR, TAF, winds aloft) use true north. Winds given by ATIS and the tower are magnetic.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What does a ceiling mean in a weather report?
options: The lowest cloud layer of any amount
The height of the lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility
questions.explain: The ceiling is the lowest layer reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC), or the vertical visibility (VV) into an obscuration.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: In a METAR, “A2992” means…
questions.explain: In the US, altimeter settings are reported in inches of mercury after the letter A.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: On a winds aloft forecast, a wind group of “9900” means…
options: Light and variable, less than 5 knots
questions.explain: 9900 means light and variable winds, less than 5 knots.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Why are some lower winds aloft entries left blank?
options: Winds are not forecast within 1,500 ft of the station elevation
questions.explain: No winds are forecast for levels within 1,500 ft of the station’s elevation, and no temperatures for the 3,000 ft level.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: An AIRMET Sierra warns of…
questions.explain: AIRMET Sierra is IFR and mountain obscuration, Tango is turbulence, strong surface winds and low-level wind shear, and Zulu is icing and freezing levels.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What does a Convective SIGMET warn about?
options: Thunderstorms and the hazards that come with them
questions.explain: Convective SIGMETs cover thunderstorm activity, which implies severe turbulence, icing and low-level wind shear.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: You fly from high pressure to low pressure without resetting your altimeter. What happens?
options: The altimeter reads lower than your true altitude
The altimeter reads higher than your true altitude, so you are lower than indicated
questions.explain: “High to low, look out below.” With a setting that’s now too high, the altimeter over-reads and you are lower than it shows.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What are standard sea-level conditions?
questions.explain: The standard atmosphere at sea level is 15 °C and 29.92 inHg (1013.25 hPa), with temperature falling about 2 °C per 1,000 ft.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What does “UUA” mean at the start of a pilot report?
questions.explain: UA is a routine pilot report. UUA is urgent, for hazards like severe turbulence, severe icing or wind shear.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Which word means “yes” in US phraseology?
questions.explain: The AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary uses AFFIRMATIVE for yes and NEGATIVE for no.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: ATC says “hold short of runway 27”. What must you do?
options: Read back the hold short instruction, including the runway
questions.explain: Pilots must read back all runway hold short instructions, including the runway designator.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: How do you say 4,500 ft on the radio?
questions.explain: Below 18,000 ft MSL, the AIM says altitudes in thousands and hundreds: “four thousand five hundred”.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Your radio fails while VFR near a towered airport. What should you do?
options: Squawk 7600, stay clear, join the pattern and watch the tower for light gun signals
questions.explain: Squawk 7600, remain outside or above the Class D, work out the active runway, join the pattern and watch the tower for light signals. Acknowledge by rocking the wings in flight.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Before takeoff, what should you set the altimeter to?
options: The current local altimeter setting, or field elevation if none is available
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.121: set the current reported altimeter setting of a station along the route within 100 NM, or the departure airport elevation if none is available.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: The static port is completely blocked. Which instruments are affected?
options: The altimeter, vertical speed indicator and airspeed indicator
questions.explain: All three pitot-static instruments use static pressure. The altimeter freezes, the VSI reads zero, and the airspeed becomes unreliable.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: In the northern hemisphere, you start a turn from a northerly heading. What does the magnetic compass do at first?
options: Shows a turn in the opposite direction, then lags
questions.explain: Turning from north, the compass initially swings the opposite way and lags behind. Turning from south it leads. Remember UNOS: undershoot north, overshoot south.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: As a private pilot, what may you accept from your passengers for a flight?
options: A pro rata share of the fuel, oil, airport fees and rental costs
Any amount they agree to pay
Payment only if the flight is longer than 50 NM
questions.explain: 14 CFR 61.113(c): a private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers, limited to fuel, oil, airport expenditures and rental fees.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: For logging night flight time, “night” is the time between…
options: One hour after sunset and one hour before sunrise
The end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight
questions.explain: 14 CFR 1.1 defines night as the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight. The one-hour-after-sunset window applies only to night passenger currency.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Between which times must an aircraft’s position lights be on?
options: End of civil twilight to start of civil twilight
One hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.209: no one may operate an aircraft between sunset and sunrise unless it has lighted position lights.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Who is responsible for briefing passengers on how to fasten and unfasten their seat belts?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.107: the pilot in command must ensure each person on board is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten their safety belt and shoulder harness.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Above what cabin pressure altitude must every occupant be provided with supplemental oxygen?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.211: above 15,000 ft MSL cabin pressure altitude, each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: How often must a transponder be tested and inspected?
options: At each annual inspection only if it has failed
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.413: a transponder must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: When does an aircraft need a 100-hour inspection as well as its annual?
options: When it carries anyone for hire or is used for flight instruction for hire
When it is flown more than 100 hours a year privately
Only if it is older than 20 years
Only if it is used at night
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.409(b): an aircraft carrying any person for hire, or provided by the person giving flight instruction for hire, needs a 100-hour inspection.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Who is primarily responsible for keeping an aircraft in an airworthy condition, including compliance with Airworthiness Directives?
options: The mechanic who last worked on it
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.403: the owner or operator is primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition, including compliance with ADs.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: How long is an aircraft registration certificate valid?
options: Until the aircraft is sold, with no expiry
questions.explain: Since 2023, 14 CFR 47.40 makes aircraft registration valid for 7 years. It also ends when the aircraft is sold.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: What is the minimum content of a flight review?
options: 1 hour of ground training and 1 hour of flight training
A written test and a medical
questions.explain: 14 CFR 61.56: at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training, reviewing Part 91 rules and the maneuvers the instructor chooses.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: A “high-performance” airplane, which needs an endorsement to act as PIC, has an engine of…
questions.explain: 14 CFR 61.31(f): a high-performance airplane has an engine of more than 200 horsepower.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: What do you need to act as pilot in command of a tailwheel airplane?
options: A separate tailwheel rating on your certificate
A one-time logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor
questions.explain: 14 CFR 61.31(i): you need training and a one-time endorsement from an authorized instructor, unless you logged PIC time in tailwheel airplanes before April 15, 1991.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Which must you have in your personal possession when acting as pilot in command?
options: Your pilot certificate, medical certificate (or BasicMed documents) and a government photo ID
questions.explain: 14 CFR 61.3: you need your pilot certificate, a current medical certificate where required, and photo identification such as a driver’s license or passport.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: May you drop an object from an aircraft in flight?
options: Yes, if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to people or property
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.15 doesn’t prohibit dropping objects if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: What is the minimum VFR fuel reserve for an airplane at night?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.151: at night there must be enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then fly for at least 45 minutes at normal cruising speed. By day it’s 30 minutes.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: For every flight, which preflight information must you become familiar with?
options: Only the weather at the destination
Runway lengths at airports of intended use and takeoff and landing distance data
Only the NOTAMs for the departure airport
The names of the controllers on duty
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.103(b): for any flight, the PIC must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance information for the aircraft.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Anywhere, what is the minimum safe altitude?
options: An altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property on the surface if a power unit fails
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.119(a): anywhere, you must be at an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard if a power unit fails.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: When may aircraft fly in formation?
options: Only by arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft in the formation
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.111: formation flight requires arrangement with the PIC of each aircraft, and passengers may not be carried for hire in formation.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: With passengers on board, when must each occupant wear an approved parachute?
options: For any intentional maneuver over 60° bank or 30° nose-up or nose-down
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.307: with passengers (other than crew), parachutes are needed for intentional maneuvers exceeding 60° of bank or 30° nose-up or nose-down, unless it’s certain flight training with an instructor.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Under NTSB 830, which injury counts as a “serious injury”?
options: Hospitalization for more than 48 hours, starting within 7 days of the injury
A visit to the emergency room
questions.explain: 49 CFR 830.2: a serious injury includes one requiring hospitalization for more than 48 hours, starting within 7 days, as well as most bone fractures and certain burns.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Under BasicMed, how often must you complete the online medical education course?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 68: the BasicMed online course every 24 calendar months, and an exam with a state-licensed physician every 48 months.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: As a student pilot flying solo by day, what minimum visibility must you have (unless your endorsement says otherwise)?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 61.89: a student pilot may not fly solo with flight or surface visibility of less than 3 SM by day or 5 SM at night.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Who may perform preventive maintenance, such as an oil change, on an aircraft you own that isn’t used for air carrier service?
options: The certificated pilot who owns or operates it, with a maintenance record entry
questions.explain: 14 CFR 43.3(g): a pilot certificated under Part 61 may perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft they own or operate (not used under Parts 121, 129 or 135) and must sign a maintenance record entry.

questions.subject: regs
questions.q: Within 30 NM of the primary airport of Class B airspace, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL, what equipment do you need?
options: An operable transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.215 and 91.225: inside the Mode C veil you need a transponder with altitude encoding and ADS-B Out, with few exceptions.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: On a sectional chart, what does a magenta shaded band (vignette) around an airport show?
options: Class E airspace starting at 700 ft AGL
questions.explain: The fuzzy side of a magenta vignette marks where Class E airspace begins at 700 ft AGL instead of 1,200 ft AGL.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: On a sectional chart, a dashed magenta line around an airport shows…
options: Class E airspace that starts at the surface
questions.explain: Dashed magenta outlines a Class E surface area. Dashed blue is Class D, solid magenta is Class C and solid blue is Class B.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: On a sectional chart, which airspace is shown with solid magenta lines?
questions.explain: Class C is drawn with solid magenta lines, Class B with solid blue lines, and Class D with dashed blue lines.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: You call Approach to enter Class C. They reply, “Aircraft calling Approach, standby.” May you enter?
options: No, they haven’t used your call sign, so communication isn’t established
questions.explain: The AIM: two-way communication is established only when the controller responds using your call sign. “Aircraft calling, standby” means stay outside.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What are the typical vertical limits of Class D airspace?
options: Surface to about 2,500 ft above the airport elevation
questions.explain: Class D normally extends from the surface to 2,500 ft above airport elevation, charted in MSL. Its lateral size varies with the airport’s instrument procedures.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What are the VFR visibility and cloud clearance minimums in Class C airspace?
options: 3 SM, 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
5 SM, 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.155: Class C, D and E below 10,000 ft MSL all need 3 SM visibility and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal from clouds.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: In Class G at night, at or below 1,200 ft AGL, flying in the traffic pattern within half a mile of the runway, what are the VFR minimums?
options: Clear of clouds, no visibility minimum
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.155(b)(2): in that case you may fly with 1 SM visibility and clear of clouds. Otherwise it’s 3 SM and 500/1,000/2,000 at night.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What are the VFR minimums in Class E airspace below 10,000 ft MSL?
options: 3 SM, 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
5 SM, 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.155: Class E below 10,000 ft MSL needs 3 SM and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: May you fly VFR in Class A airspace?
options: No, all flight in Class A must be under IFR
Only with a clearance from Center
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.135: operations in Class A airspace (18,000 ft MSL to FL600) must be conducted under IFR.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What is a prohibited area, such as P-56 over Washington, DC?
options: Airspace where flight is allowed with permission from the controlling agency
Airspace where aircraft may not fly, for security or national welfare reasons
An area of high training activity
An area of military exercises over water
questions.explain: The AIM: flight within a prohibited area isn’t allowed. Restricted areas may be entered with permission when not active, or as allowed by the controlling agency.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What is a warning area?
options: Airspace starting 3 NM from the US coast that may contain hazards to non-participating aircraft
Airspace where VFR flight is banned
An area where parachute jumping takes place
questions.explain: The AIM: a warning area extends from 3 NM outward from the coast and contains activity that may be hazardous to non-participating aircraft.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What should you do when flying through an alert area?
options: Get permission from the controlling agency first
Nothing special is required, but be especially alert for high volumes of training or unusual activity
questions.explain: The AIM: alert areas contain a high volume of pilot training or unusual activity. All pilots are equally responsible for collision avoidance there.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: How do you find out about a temporary flight restriction (TFR) before a flight?
options: They’re printed on the sectional chart
Check NOTAMs during your preflight briefing
They only apply to IFR flights
questions.explain: TFRs are issued by NOTAM, so you need to check NOTAMs (for example during an official preflight briefing) before every flight.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: Over national wildlife refuges and parks, pilots are asked to stay at least how high?
questions.explain: the AIM asks pilots to keep at least 2,000 ft above the surface over national parks, wildlife refuges and similar areas.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: You’re VFR more than 3,000 ft AGL on a magnetic course of 220°. Which is an appropriate cruising altitude?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.159: magnetic courses 180° to 359° use even thousands plus 500 ft, so 6,500 ft. Odd thousands plus 500 ft, like 5,500, are for 0° to 179°.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: In a sectional chart quadrangle, what does a large number like 3⁵ show?
options: The maximum elevation figure: 3,500 ft MSL clears the highest terrain and obstacles in that quadrangle
questions.explain: The maximum elevation figure (MEF) is in thousands and hundreds of feet MSL and is set above the highest terrain or obstacle in that quadrangle.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: Next to an obstacle on a sectional you see 1549 in bold and (749) below it. What do they mean?
options: 1,549 ft MSL height of the top, 749 ft AGL height
questions.explain: The bold figure is the top of the obstacle above mean sea level; the figure in parentheses is its height above ground level.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: On a sectional, an airport’s information shows “CT – 118.3 ★”. What does the star mean?
questions.explain: CT is the control tower frequency, and the star means the tower operates part-time. Check the Chart Supplement for its hours.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: On a sectional, why is one airport symbol blue and another magenta?
options: Blue is a paved runway, magenta is grass
Blue has a control tower, magenta has no tower
Blue is military, magenta is civil
questions.explain: Airports with an operating control tower are blue; airports without one are magenta.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What does a Military Training Route labeled “VR1234” (four digits) tell you?
options: It’s flown under IFR above 1,500 ft AGL
It’s flown VFR at or below 1,500 ft AGL along its whole length
questions.explain: VR means VFR military training. Four digits mean no segment is above 1,500 ft AGL; three digits mean one or more segments are above 1,500 ft AGL.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: As a student pilot, what do you need to fly solo in Class B airspace?
options: Ground and flight training plus a specific logbook endorsement
questions.explain: 14 CFR 61.95: a student needs training and an endorsement for that specific Class B airspace. Some Class B primary airports don’t allow student solo takeoffs and landings at all.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What is the speed limit in a VFR corridor through Class B, or under a Class B shelf?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.117(c): no more than 200 knots in airspace underlying Class B or in a VFR corridor through it.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: What do you need to fly special VFR at night?
options: An instrument rating and an aircraft equipped for IFR
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.157: special VFR at night requires the pilot to be instrument rated and current and the aircraft to be IFR-equipped.

questions.subject: airspace
questions.q: Within the surface area of Class D airspace, what weather do you need to take off or land VFR without a special VFR clearance?
options: Ceiling at least 1,000 ft and visibility at least 3 SM
Any weather, if you stay clear of clouds
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.155(c) and (d): within surface areas of controlled airspace, VFR needs a ceiling of at least 1,000 ft and ground visibility of at least 3 SM.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What does a yellow “ladder” marking across a taxiway, with a matching sign, show?
options: The hold position for the ILS critical area
questions.explain: The ILS critical area hold position marking looks like a ladder. Hold there when ATC tells you to, so you don’t disturb the ILS signal.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What does a yellow sign showing the hold-position marking lines (runway boundary sign) tell you as you exit a runway?
options: Once you’re past it, you’re clear of the runway
questions.explain: The runway boundary sign faces the runway and marks the point you must pass to be clear of it.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: A sign with a black background, a yellow border and a yellow letter “B” means…
questions.explain: A location sign (black with yellow letters) tells you which taxiway or runway you are on.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What does a red sign with a white circle and a horizontal white bar mean?
questions.explain: The no-entry sign marks paved areas aircraft must not enter, such as one-way taxiways or areas meant for vehicles.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What color are taxiway edge lights?
questions.explain: Taxiway edge lights are blue. Taxiway centerline lights, where installed, are green.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What do runway end identifier lights (REIL) look like?
options: A row of steady green lights
A pair of synchronized flashing lights at each side of the threshold
questions.explain: REIL are two synchronized flashing lights either side of the threshold, to help you pick out the runway end.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: From the approach end, what color are the runway threshold lights?
questions.explain: Threshold lights show green toward an approaching aircraft and red toward an aircraft on the runway, marking the runway end.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: With radio-controlled runway lighting, how do you usually select the highest intensity?
options: Key the microphone 3 times in 5 seconds
Key the microphone 5 times in 5 seconds
Key the microphone 7 times in 5 seconds
Call the tower on the CTAF
questions.explain: The AIM: 7 clicks within 5 seconds for high intensity, 5 for medium, 3 for low.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: At a segmented circle, what do the L-shaped markers next to it show?
options: The direction of turns in the traffic pattern for each runway
questions.explain: The L-shaped traffic pattern indicators show whether the pattern for each runway uses left or right turns.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: At about what wind speed is a typical wind sock fully extended?
questions.explain: FAA wind cone standards (AC 150/5345-27) call for a wind cone to be fully extended at about 15 knots.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: How is a closed runway marked?
options: A yellow X at each end
A white X at each end
questions.explain: A closed runway has a white X at each end (often a lighted X). Closed taxiways are marked with a yellow X.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What traffic pattern altitude does the AIM recommend for light propeller airplanes, unless published otherwise?
questions.explain: the AIM recommends 1,000 ft above airport elevation for propeller-driven aircraft unless established otherwise.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: How should you depart the traffic pattern at a nontowered airport?
options: Continue straight out, or turn 45° in the direction of the pattern after reaching pattern altitude
Make a 180° turn over the runway
Climb overhead the airport before leaving
questions.explain: The AIM: depart straight out or with a 45° turn in the direction of the pattern, beyond the departure end of the runway, after reaching pattern altitude.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: Should a student pilot accept a land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance?
options: No, student pilots shouldn’t take part in LAHSO
Only on runways longer than 5,000 ft
questions.explain: The AIM: student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate. Any pilot may decline a LAHSO clearance.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: How far should you stay away from a hovering helicopter while taxiing?
options: It doesn’t matter if you’re upwind
questions.explain: The AIM’s wake turbulence section advises: avoid operating within three rotor diameters of a hovering helicopter, whose downwash is strong.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: Tower tells you “line up and wait, runway 27”. What do you do?
options: Taxi onto runway 27, line up, and wait for a takeoff clearance
questions.explain: “Line up and wait” lets you enter the runway and line up, but you’re not cleared for takeoff.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: Tower says “cleared for the option”. What may you do?
options: A touch-and-go, low approach, missed approach, stop-and-go or full stop, at your choice
questions.explain: The AIM: the option lets you choose any of those maneuvers.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What is the purpose of ATIS?
options: To give you a taxi clearance
To broadcast recorded noncontrol information such as weather, active runway and NOTAMs, so controllers can focus on traffic
To give you a squawk code
questions.explain: ATIS repeats routine information. Tell the controller on first contact which ATIS letter you have.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: When taxiing at a towered airport, what do you need before crossing a runway?
options: Nothing if your taxi route crosses it
An explicit clearance to cross that runway
questions.explain: You need a specific clearance for each runway you cross. A taxi clearance to a runway doesn’t authorize crossing others along the way.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What color does a tri-color VASI show when you’re on the glide path?
questions.explain: A tri-color VASI shows amber above the glide path, green on it, and red below it.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What is a “hot spot” on an airport diagram?
options: A place with hot exhaust from jets
A location with a history of, or risk of, collisions or runway incursions
questions.explain: Hot spots are marked on airport diagrams where pilots and drivers need extra attention, often complex intersections.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: What does an enhanced taxiway centerline (dashed yellow lines either side of the solid centerline) warn you of?
options: An upcoming runway holding position marking
questions.explain: Enhanced centerline markings run up to 150 ft before a runway holding position to warn you a runway is close.

questions.subject: airport
questions.q: Do you need an ATC clearance to taxi in the non-movement area, such as the ramp?
options: No, but take care; ATC clearance is needed once you enter the movement area
Only if a tower is open
questions.explain: The non-movement area boundary is a solid and dashed yellow line. ATC clearance is needed only on the movement area side.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Wingtip vortices from a large aircraft tend to…
options: Sink at several hundred feet per minute and level off about 500 to 900 ft below its flight path
Stay at the same level indefinitely
questions.explain: The AIM: vortices sink at a few hundred feet per minute, slowing and leveling off around 500 to 900 ft below the generating aircraft’s path.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: When does a departing large aircraft start producing wake turbulence?
options: As soon as the engines start
When its nose wheel lifts off at rotation
When it retracts its landing gear
questions.explain: Vortices begin when the wing starts producing lift at rotation. Lift off before that point and climb above its path.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: How long does a typical microburst last?
questions.explain: The AIM: microbursts seldom last more than 15 minutes, but their downdrafts can reach 6,000 ft per minute.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: During engine start, the induction system catches fire. What do most light-aircraft checklists say to do?
options: Stop cranking immediately and get out
Keep cranking the engine to draw the fire into it
Open the throttle fully and pump the primer
Turn off the master and wait
questions.explain: Most POH checklists say to continue cranking so the fire is drawn into the engine, then follow the rest of the fire checklist. Always use your aircraft’s POH.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: With a fixed-pitch propeller, what is the first sign of carburetor ice?
questions.explain: With a fixed-pitch propeller, carburetor ice first shows as a drop in RPM, often followed by rough running.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: A fuel sample from an avgas airplane is clear and smells like kerosene. What does that suggest?
options: Possible jet fuel contamination; don’t fly until it’s resolved
Fuel that has been too cold
questions.explain: 100LL is blue. Clear, kerosene-smelling fuel suggests Jet A, which can cause detonation and engine failure in piston engines.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Taxiing a tricycle-gear airplane with a quartering headwind from the left, how should you hold the controls?
options: Left aileron up (yoke turned left), elevator neutral
questions.explain: Turn the yoke into the wind (raising the upwind aileron) and keep the elevator neutral for a tricycle-gear airplane in a quartering headwind.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Taxiing with a quartering tailwind from the left, how should you hold the controls?
options: Yoke turned right (left aileron down), elevator down
questions.explain: With a quartering tailwind, “dive away” from the wind: aileron down on the upwind side and elevator down.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: What is the aim of a soft-field takeoff technique?
options: To lift off at the highest possible speed
To keep weight off the nosewheel and get airborne as soon as possible, then accelerate in ground effect
To stay on the ground as long as possible
To use full flaps and a steep climb immediately
questions.explain: Holding back pressure transfers weight to the wing quickly. Once airborne, stay in ground effect to build speed before climbing.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: At night, you see a steady red light and a flashing red light ahead at your altitude. What is the other aircraft doing?
options: Crossing from your right to your left
Crossing from your left to your right
questions.explain: The red position light is on the left wingtip. Seeing only red means the aircraft’s left side faces you, so it is moving from your right to your left.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: At night you see steady red and green lights ahead at your altitude. What is the other aircraft doing?
questions.explain: Seeing both wingtip lights (red on its left, green on its right) at once means the aircraft is coming toward you. Take avoiding action.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: When may you test an ELT?
options: Only during the first 5 minutes after the hour, for no more than 3 audio sweeps
Only with Flight Service on the phone
questions.explain: The AIM: ground tests should be done in the first 5 minutes after any hour, limited to three audio sweeps.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Before starting the engine, why should you shout “clear prop”?
options: To warn anyone nearby and make sure nobody is near the propeller
questions.explain: Always check the area and call “clear” so nobody is near the propeller. Never hand-prop without a competent person at the controls.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Your VFR flight plan is open and you forget to close it. What happens?
options: Search and rescue starts if it isn’t closed within about 30 minutes after your ETA
The flight plan closes itself on landing
questions.explain: The AIM: if a VFR flight plan isn’t closed within 30 minutes of the ETA, search and rescue procedures begin.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: What is VFR flight following?
options: Mandatory radar service for every VFR flight
Optional radar traffic advisories ATC gives VFR pilots when workload permits
questions.explain: Flight following is optional, workload permitting, and doesn’t relieve you of see-and-avoid or terrain clearance.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: As a VFR pilot, you accidentally fly into cloud. What should you do?
options: Descend quickly to find the ground
Trust the instruments, keep the wings level, and make a gentle 180° turn back to VFR conditions
questions.explain: Rely on the flight instruments, not your senses, and make a shallow, standard-rate 180° turn back to where you came from. Ask ATC for help if needed.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Why do you make clearing turns before practicing maneuvers?
options: To check for other traffic around and below you
questions.explain: Clearing turns let you look for traffic in the area you’re about to maneuver through.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: During a go-around, what should you do first?
options: Raise all the flaps at once
Apply full power, stop the descent and pitch for a climb
Call the tower before anything else
questions.explain: Power first, then stop the descent, then clean up drag (flaps in stages) and climb at the recommended speed. Aviate, then communicate.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: When should the anticollision lights be on?
options: During all operations, day and night, unless the PIC turns them off for safety
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.209: if installed, anticollision lights must be on during all operations, except the PIC may turn them off when it’s safer to do so.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Why use a written checklist even on a familiar airplane?
options: It makes sure no important step is missed, however familiar the routine
questions.explain: Checklists catch steps that are easy to miss when you’re distracted, rushed or complacent.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: On the ground you see a steady green light from the tower. What does it mean?
questions.explain: Steady green on the ground means cleared for takeoff. Flashing green on the ground means cleared to taxi.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: In flight you see a flashing green light from the tower. What does it mean?
options: Return for landing, to be followed by a steady green at the proper time
questions.explain: Flashing green in flight means return for landing; a steady green then clears you to land.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: On the ground you see a flashing red light from the tower. What should you do?
options: Taxi clear of the runway in use
questions.explain: Flashing red on the ground means taxi clear of the runway in use. Steady red means stop.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: What does an alternating red and green light from the tower mean?
questions.explain: Alternating red and green, in the air or on the ground, means exercise extreme caution.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Which aircraft has right of way over all the others listed?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.113: a balloon has right of way over every other category of aircraft (except an aircraft in distress).

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Which aircraft has right of way over all other air traffic?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.113(c): an aircraft in distress has right of way over all other air traffic.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: An airplane towing a glider and another airplane are converging. Who has right of way?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.113(d): aircraft towing or refueling other aircraft have right of way over all other engine-driven aircraft.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Two aircraft are on final to land. The lower one has right of way. What must it not do?
options: Take advantage of that rule to cut in front of another aircraft on final
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.113(g): the lower aircraft has right of way but may not use that rule to cut in front of or overtake another aircraft on final.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: When changing your transponder code in flight, which codes should you avoid passing through?
questions.explain: The AIM: avoid inadvertently selecting 7500, 7600 or 7700 while changing codes, as they trigger alarms at ATC facilities.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: What do you need before flying VFR within 60 NM of the Washington, DC (DCA) VOR?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.161: pilots flying VFR within 60 NM of the DCA VOR/DME must complete the FAA special awareness training.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: In an in-flight emergency needing immediate action, what may the pilot in command do?
options: Deviate from any rule in Part 91 to the extent needed to meet the emergency
Nothing until a report is filed
Declare an emergency only once on the ground
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.3(b): the PIC may deviate from any Part 91 rule to the extent required. A written report may be requested afterwards.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: ATC gives you priority in an emergency. What might you have to do afterwards?
options: Submit a detailed report within 48 hours if ATC requests it
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.123(d): a pilot given priority may be asked to submit a detailed report within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: You get an ATC clearance you can’t safely follow. What should you do?
options: Tell ATC “unable” and get an amended clearance
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.123: you must follow a clearance once accepted, so if you can’t comply, say “unable” and get an amended one. In an emergency you may deviate, and must tell ATC as soon as possible.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Flying VFR while receiving radar service, who is responsible for seeing and avoiding other aircraft?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.113(b): when weather permits, each pilot must see and avoid other aircraft, whether or not under ATC control.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: A military aircraft intercepts you, rocks its wings and makes a slow turn. What does it mean, and how do you respond?
options: “You may proceed”; wave and carry on
“You have been intercepted, follow me”; rock your wings and follow
“Land immediately”; lower the gear at once
questions.explain: The AIM: rocking wings means “you have been intercepted, follow me”. Rock your wings to acknowledge, follow, and try to contact the interceptor on 121.5.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: If you are intercepted, which transponder code should you select unless told otherwise?
questions.explain: The AIM: select 7700 unless otherwise instructed by air traffic services.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: A METAR shows “VV004”. What does it mean?
options: Vertical visibility 400 ft into an indefinite ceiling
questions.explain: VV is vertical visibility into an obscuration. It counts as a ceiling, here 400 ft.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What does “-RA BR” mean in a METAR?
questions.explain: The minus sign means light, RA is rain, and BR is mist (from the French “brume”).

questions.subject: met
questions.q: A METAR reports “SCT015 BKN030 OVC050”. What is the ceiling?
questions.explain: The ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer (or vertical visibility). Scattered doesn’t count, so it’s BKN030: 3,000 ft above ground.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What does “AO2” in the remarks of a METAR mean?
options: An automated station with a precipitation sensor
questions.explain: AO2 is an automated station that can tell types of precipitation apart. AO1 has no precipitation discriminator.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: A METAR shows “M02/M05”. What does it tell you?
questions.explain: M means minus. Temperature −2°C, dew point −5°C.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: In a TAF, what does “FM1500” mean?
options: From 1500Z, a rapid change to these conditions
questions.explain: FM (from) marks a rapid, significant change starting at that time, in UTC (Zulu).

questions.subject: met
questions.q: In a TAF, what does “PROB30” mean?
options: A 30% probability of the conditions that follow
questions.explain: PROB30 gives a 30% chance of the following weather, usually thunderstorms or precipitation, in that period.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What time zone are METAR and TAF times given in?
questions.explain: Aviation weather reports and forecasts use Coordinated Universal Time, shown with a Z.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: A winds aloft forecast for 39,000 ft shows “731960”. What is the forecast wind and temperature?
questions.explain: A direction over 36 means subtract 50 from it and add 100 to the speed: 73−50 = 230°, 19+100 = 119 kt. Above 24,000 ft temperatures are always negative: −60°C.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: ATIS and tower wind reports are given relative to…
questions.explain: Wind given by ATIS and controllers is in magnetic, to match runway headings. METARs, TAFs and winds aloft use true north.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: An AIRMET Tango warns of…
options: Moderate turbulence, surface winds of 30 knots or more, or low-level wind shear
questions.explain: AIRMET Sierra is IFR and mountain obscuration, Tango is turbulence, strong surface winds and LLWS, and Zulu is icing and freezing levels.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: An AIRMET Zulu warns of…
questions.explain: Zulu covers moderate icing and the height of the freezing level.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: A (non-convective) SIGMET is issued for…
options: Severe icing, severe or extreme turbulence, dust or sandstorms below 3 SM, or volcanic ash
questions.explain: SIGMETs cover hazards dangerous to all aircraft, including severe icing and severe or extreme turbulence.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What weather is typical of unstable air?
options: Cumuliform clouds, showery precipitation, turbulence and good visibility outside showers
questions.explain: Unstable air rises readily, building cumulus, showers and bumpy air, with good visibility outside the showers.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What weather is typical of stable air?
options: Stratiform clouds, steady precipitation, smooth air and poor visibility
questions.explain: Stable air resists lifting, giving layered clouds, steady precipitation, smooth air and often haze or fog.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What does a temperature inversion near the ground usually bring?
options: Smooth air with poor visibility below it
questions.explain: In an inversion, temperature rises with height. Air below it is stable, trapping haze, smoke and fog.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What is the dew point?
options: The temperature at which the air becomes saturated when cooled
The temperature of the ground at dawn
questions.explain: Cool air to its dew point and it becomes saturated, so cloud, fog or dew can form.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: The surface temperature is 26°C and the dew point is 16°C. Roughly where will the base of convective clouds be?
questions.explain: Divide the temperature–dew point spread by 2.5°C per 1,000 ft: 10 ÷ 2.5 = 4, so about 4,000 ft AGL.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Which three things does a thunderstorm need to form?
options: Wind, cold air and low pressure
Sufficient moisture, an unstable lapse rate and a lifting force
High pressure, sunshine and dry air
A warm front, fog and calm wind
questions.explain: Thunderstorms need moist air, instability, and something to start lifting it, such as heating, terrain or a front.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What characterizes the cumulus stage of a thunderstorm?
questions.explain: In the cumulus stage, updrafts dominate. The mature stage starts when precipitation reaches the ground with both up and downdrafts. Downdrafts dominate the dissipating stage.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: How far should you stay from a severe thunderstorm?
options: It’s fine to fly under it
questions.explain: The AIM: avoid severe thunderstorms by at least 20 NM. Hail can fall far from the storm itself.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What is a squall line?
options: A line of fog along a coast
A narrow band of active thunderstorms, often ahead of a cold front
questions.explain: A squall line is a non-frontal line of thunderstorms, often ahead of a cold front, and one of the most dangerous weather features for aircraft.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Why must frost be removed from the wings before flight?
options: It adds a lot of weight
It disrupts the smooth airflow, which can raise the stall speed and stop the airplane flying
questions.explain: Even a thin layer of frost roughens the wing surface, cutting lift and raising stall speed. Remove it all before takeoff.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Ice pellets at the surface tell you there is…
options: Freezing rain at a higher altitude, with warmer air above
questions.explain: Rain falling from a warmer layer freezes in colder air below. Ice pellets mean freezing rain is probably falling somewhere above.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Standing lenticular clouds downwind of mountains suggest…
options: Mountain waves and possible strong turbulence
questions.explain: Lenticular clouds mark mountain wave activity, which can bring severe turbulence and strong up and downdrafts.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What weather usually comes with a warm front?
options: Stratiform clouds, steady precipitation and poor visibility over a wide area
questions.explain: Warm air sliding over cooler air produces widespread layered clouds and steady rain or drizzle, sometimes fog.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: On a surface analysis chart, isobars close together mean…
questions.explain: The closer the isobars, the steeper the pressure gradient and the stronger the wind.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Why does the surface wind differ in speed and direction from the wind a couple of thousand feet up?
options: Ground friction slows it and changes its direction
The Coriolis force is stronger near the ground
questions.explain: Friction with the surface slows the wind near the ground, weakening the Coriolis effect so the wind backs across the isobars.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Which type of weather briefing should you ask for if you’re leaving in more than 6 hours?
questions.explain: An outlook briefing is for departures 6 or more hours away. Ask for a standard briefing nearer the time.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Which conditions are reported as marginal VFR (MVFR)?
options: Ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 ft and/or visibility 3 to 5 SM
Ceiling above 3,000 ft and visibility above 5 SM
questions.explain: MVFR is ceiling 1,000–3,000 ft and/or visibility 3–5 SM. IFR is below 1,000 ft or 3 SM.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Upslope fog forms when…
options: Warm air moves over cold water
Moist, stable air is pushed up sloping terrain and cools to its dew point
The ground cools on a clear night
questions.explain: Moist, stable air cooled as it rises up a slope forms upslope fog, which can be deep and long-lasting.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Where is clear air turbulence often found?
options: Near the surface on calm days
Near the jet stream at high altitude
questions.explain: Clear air turbulence is common near the jet stream, where wind shear is strong.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What should your first call to an ATC facility include?
options: Who you’re calling, who you are, where you are, and what you want
Your fuel on board and souls on board
questions.explain: The AIM: start with the facility you’re calling and your full call sign, then your position and request.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: How do you say “N723AB” on the radio?
questions.explain: Use the phonetic alphabet for letters and say each number separately.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: How should the number 9 be said on the radio?
questions.explain: The AIM uses “niner” so it isn’t confused with the German “nein”.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: When may you use an abbreviated call sign, such as “3AB”?
options: Only after ATC has used it first
questions.explain: The AIM: use your full call sign on first contact. You may abbreviate only after the controller does.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: At a nontowered airport with no tower, FSS or UNICOM, which frequency do you use as the CTAF?
questions.explain: The AIM: with no tower, FSS or UNICOM, self-announce on MULTICOM 122.9.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: How should a self-announce call at a nontowered airport begin and end?
options: With the airport name and “traffic”, repeated at the end
questions.explain: For example: “Pine Bluff traffic, Cessna 3AB, left downwind runway 18, Pine Bluff.” Saying the airport name at the end confirms where you are.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: ATC says “traffic, two o’clock, three miles, eastbound”. The two o’clock position is relative to…
questions.explain: Traffic positions are based on your ground track as seen on radar. With a crosswind correction, adjust where you look.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What does “UNABLE” mean?
options: I can’t comply with your instruction
questions.explain: Say “unable” when you can’t comply with an instruction or clearance, then explain if you can.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Which ATC instructions must you read back?
options: Hold-short instructions, runway assignments, altitudes, headings and frequencies
questions.explain: Read back runway hold-short instructions in full, and runway, altitude and heading assignments, ending with your call sign.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What does “radar contact” mean?
options: ATC will keep you clear of terrain and all traffic
Your aircraft is identified on radar, and you’ll get radar services such as traffic advisories
questions.explain: “Radar contact” means you’re identified. As a VFR pilot you’re still responsible for see-and-avoid and terrain clearance.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What does “resume own navigation” mean?
options: Return to the airport you left
You’re responsible for your own navigation again, for example after radar vectors
questions.explain: ATC uses it after radar vectors or if radar contact is lost while vectoring: navigation is back with you.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: ATC says “radar service terminated, squawk VFR”. What do you do?
questions.explain: In the US, the VFR code is 1200. Keep it on with altitude reporting.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: At airports with Class B or C airspace, whom do you often call before ground control?
questions.explain: At many busier airports, call clearance delivery first for your departure frequency, squawk and altitude, then ground for taxi.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What is UNICOM?
options: A nongovernment air-ground station giving airport advisory information
questions.explain: UNICOM is run by an FBO or airport operator and provides advisory information like fuel and runway in use. It isn’t ATC.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What does “EXPEDITE” mean?
options: Prompt compliance is needed to avoid an imminent situation
questions.explain: Expedite means comply promptly. If you can’t, tell ATC.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: ATC tells you to “climb and maintain 3,500”. How do you read it back?
options: “Climb and maintain three thousand five hundred, November 3AB”
questions.explain: Read back the altitude and end with your call sign so ATC knows who answered.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: According to Bernoulli’s principle, as air speeds up over the curved top of a wing, its pressure…
options: Becomes equal to the pressure below
questions.explain: Faster-moving air has lower static pressure. The pressure difference between upper and lower surfaces is part of how a wing makes lift.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Can an airplane stall at any airspeed and in any attitude?
options: No, only when the nose is high
Yes, whenever the critical angle of attack is exceeded
questions.explain: A stall depends only on exceeding the critical angle of attack, which can happen at any airspeed, attitude or power setting.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: In a level 60° banked turn, by how much does the stall speed increase?
questions.explain: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor. At 60° the load factor is 2, and √2 ≈ 1.41, so about 41% higher.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: In a level 45° banked turn, what is the load factor?
questions.explain: Load factor in a level turn is 1 ÷ cos(bank). At 45°, 1 ÷ 0.707 ≈ 1.41 G.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: How does design maneuvering speed (VA) change as the airplane gets lighter?
questions.explain: A lighter airplane can be accelerated to its load limit more easily, so its maneuvering speed is lower.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: On the airspeed indicator, the bottom of the white arc is…
options: VSO, stall speed in the landing configuration
questions.explain: The white arc is the flap operating range: its bottom is VSO (landing configuration stall speed) and its top is VFE.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: On the airspeed indicator, the bottom of the green arc is…
options: VS1, stall speed in a specified configuration (usually flaps up)
questions.explain: The green arc is the normal operating range, from VS1 to VNO.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: What does the yellow arc on the airspeed indicator mean?
options: Caution range: fly there only in smooth air
questions.explain: The yellow arc runs from VNO to VNE. Fly in it only in smooth air, and with caution.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: What causes P-factor at high angles of attack, such as in a climb?
options: The descending propeller blade on the right taking a bigger bite of air than the ascending one, yawing the airplane left
questions.explain: At high angles of attack, the descending right-side blade has a greater angle of attack and more thrust, which yaws the nose left (for a clockwise-turning propeller seen from the cockpit).

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: How does dihedral help the airplane?
questions.explain: Dihedral helps a wing that drops in a sideslip produce more lift, rolling the airplane back toward level.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: In a steep turn, why do you often need some opposite aileron?
options: Because of the overbanking tendency: the outer wing travels faster and makes more lift
questions.explain: In steep turns, the outside wing moves faster than the inside one, creating more lift and a tendency to roll further into the bank.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Climbing out of ground effect, what happens to induced drag?
options: It increases, so the airplane may sink or fail to climb if it lifted off too slowly
questions.explain: In ground effect, induced drag is reduced. Leaving it, induced drag rises, which is dangerous if you lifted off below the recommended speed.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: In a turn, the ball in the turn coordinator is out to the inside of the turn. What’s happening?
options: A skidding turn: too much rudder
A slipping turn: not enough rudder for the bank
questions.explain: A slip leaves the ball on the inside of the turn. Step on the ball (add rudder on that side) to coordinate.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: What is the typical spin recovery for most light airplanes (PARE)?
options: Power idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, elevator forward to break the stall
Ailerons into the spin and full power
questions.explain: PARE: Power to idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder full opposite to the rotation, Elevator briskly forward. Always follow the POH.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Best glide speed is the speed at which the airplane…
options: Has the lowest total drag (the best lift-to-drag ratio)
questions.explain: Best glide speed corresponds to L/D max, the point of lowest total drag, giving the greatest distance per foot of altitude lost.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Gliding into a strong headwind after an engine failure, to cover the most ground you should…
options: Fly somewhat faster than best glide
Keep exactly best glide at all times
questions.explain: Into a headwind, a slightly higher speed reduces the time the wind acts on you and improves distance over the ground.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: What is the angle of incidence?
options: The angle between the chord line and the relative wind
The fixed angle between the wing’s chord line and the airplane’s longitudinal axis
questions.explain: Angle of incidence is set when the wing is built. Angle of attack is the one that changes in flight.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: The elevator controls the airplane’s movement about which axis?
questions.explain: The elevator controls pitch about the lateral axis. Ailerons control roll about the longitudinal axis, and the rudder controls yaw about the vertical axis.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Why do many wings have washout (the tip twisted to a lower angle of incidence than the root)?
options: So the root stalls first and the ailerons keep working near the stall
questions.explain: With washout, the wing root reaches the critical angle first, keeping airflow over the ailerons for roll control.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: What are the load factor limits for a normal-category airplane?
questions.explain: Normal category: +3.8 and −1.52 G. Utility: +4.4 and −1.76 G. Acrobatic: +6.0 and −3.0 G.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Why does the left-turning tendency need the most right rudder during takeoff and climb?
options: High power and low airspeed make torque, P-factor and the spiraling slipstream strongest
questions.explain: At high power and low speed, all left-turning tendencies are at their strongest, so you need right rudder to stay straight.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: How does high humidity affect density altitude and performance?
options: It lowers density altitude and improves performance
It raises density altitude and slightly reduces performance
It only affects the engine’s cooling
questions.explain: Water vapor is lighter than dry air, so humid air is less dense: density altitude rises and performance drops slightly.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: How do you find pressure altitude?
options: Read the altimeter with the current local setting
Set 29.92 inHg in the altimeter window and read the altitude
questions.explain: Pressure altitude is the altitude shown with the altimeter set to the standard 29.92 inHg.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Field elevation is 1,000 ft and the altimeter setting is 30.42. What is the pressure altitude?

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Pressure altitude is 3,000 ft and the temperature is 29°C. Roughly what is the density altitude?
questions.explain: Standard temperature at 3,000 ft is about 9°C. 20°C above standard × 120 ft = 2,400 ft. 3,000 + 2,400 ≈ 5,400 ft.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Which speed gives the greatest gain in altitude over a given distance, for example to clear an obstacle?
questions.explain: VX is best angle of climb (most altitude per distance). VY is best rate of climb (most altitude per unit of time).

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Which speed gives the greatest gain in altitude in the shortest time?
questions.explain: VY, best rate of climb, gives the most altitude per minute.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: An airplane weighs 2,000 lb with a total moment of 180,000 lb-in. Where is its center of gravity?
questions.explain: CG = total moment ÷ total weight = 180,000 ÷ 2,000 = 90 in.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: An airplane weighs 2,500 lb. You move a 50 lb bag 100 inches aft. How far does the CG move?
questions.explain: Weight moved ÷ total weight = CG change ÷ distance moved. 50 ÷ 2,500 × 100 = 2 in aft.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: About how much does 40 US gallons of avgas weigh?
questions.explain: Avgas weighs about 6 lb per US gallon, so 40 × 6 = 240 lb.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: What is the useful load of an airplane?
options: The difference between maximum gross weight and basic empty weight: people, baggage and usable fuel
Only the weight of the fuel
questions.explain: Useful load is what you can add to the basic empty weight, including pilot, passengers, baggage and usable fuel.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: What does basic empty weight include?
options: The airframe, engine, fixed equipment, unusable fuel, and full operating fluids including oil
questions.explain: Basic empty weight includes unusable fuel, full hydraulic fluid and full engine oil, along with standard and optional equipment.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: The wind is 15 knots at 45° to the runway. Roughly what is the crosswind component?
questions.explain: Crosswind = wind speed × sin(angle). sin 45° ≈ 0.7, so 15 × 0.7 ≈ 11 knots.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: You’re landing on runway 36 with the wind from 330° at 20 knots. Roughly what is the crosswind component?
questions.explain: The wind is 30° off the runway. sin 30° = 0.5, so 20 × 0.5 = 10 knots.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: What is the maximum demonstrated crosswind component in the POH?
options: A legal limit you can never exceed
The highest crosswind shown during certification, not necessarily a limit
The crosswind at which the airplane will tip over
questions.explain: It’s the strongest crosswind tested during certification. It isn’t a limitation, but your own skill may set a lower one.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: According to the FAA, increasing takeoff weight by 10% increases takeoff distance by at least about…
questions.explain: The PHAK notes a 10% heavier airplane needs about 5% more takeoff speed, has at least 9% less acceleration, and needs at least 21% more takeoff distance.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: For maximum endurance (longest time aloft), you should fly at…
options: The speed for minimum power required (lowest fuel flow)
questions.explain: Maximum endurance is at minimum power required. Maximum range is near the L/D max speed.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Your airplane burns 8 gal/hr. For a 3-hour day VFR flight, what is the minimum fuel including the required reserve?
questions.explain: 3 h × 8 = 24 gal, plus 30 minutes’ reserve by day (4 gal) = 28 gal. More margin is wise.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: How does flying above maximum weight affect stall speed?
questions.explain: A heavier airplane needs a higher angle of attack for a given speed, so it reaches the critical angle at a higher airspeed.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: A POH’s “total distance to clear a 50 ft obstacle” includes…
options: The ground roll plus the distance to climb to 50 ft
questions.explain: Takeoff charts often show both the ground roll and the total distance including the climb to 50 ft above the runway.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Your true airspeed is 110 knots and you have a 20-knot headwind. What is your groundspeed?
questions.explain: With a direct headwind, groundspeed = TAS − headwind = 110 − 20 = 90 knots.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: What is true altitude?
options: Altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature only
questions.explain: True altitude is your actual height above MSL. Absolute altitude is height above ground level.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: What is absolute altitude?
options: Height above the ground directly below
The altitude shown on the altimeter
questions.explain: Absolute altitude is your height above the terrain (AGL).

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: You fly into much colder than standard air without changing the altimeter setting. Compared with what’s indicated, your true altitude is…
questions.explain: “From hot to cold, look out below.” In colder air, the altimeter over-reads, so you’re lower than indicated.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: You change the altimeter setting from 29.90 to 30.00. What happens to the indicated altitude?
questions.explain: Each 0.01 inHg is about 10 ft. Increasing the setting by 0.10 raises the indicated altitude by about 100 ft.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Which pressure source does the vertical speed indicator use?
questions.explain: The VSI compares current static pressure with static pressure trapped behind a calibrated leak.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Which principle does the attitude indicator rely on?
questions.explain: The attitude indicator’s gyro stays fixed in space while the airplane moves around it.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: A standard-rate turn is…
options: 3° per second, a full 360° in 2 minutes
questions.explain: A standard-rate turn is 3° per second. The turn coordinator’s marks show it.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: What does the turn coordinator show that the older turn-and-slip indicator doesn’t?
options: The rate of roll as well as rate of turn
questions.explain: Its gyro is canted, so it responds to roll as well as yaw, showing rate of roll and rate of turn.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: The pitot tube’s ram air inlet is blocked but its drain hole stays open. What does the airspeed indicator do?
questions.explain: Pressure in the pitot line drains out until it matches static pressure, so the airspeed indicator falls to zero.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: You select the alternate static source inside the cabin. What usually happens to the instruments?
options: The altimeter and airspeed read slightly higher than normal
questions.explain: Cabin pressure is usually a little lower than outside, so the altimeter and airspeed read slightly high and the VSI briefly shows a climb.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: What are the four strokes of a piston engine?
questions.explain: The four-stroke cycle is intake, compression, power and exhaust.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: During the magneto check, switching to one magneto gives no RPM drop at all. What could that mean?
options: A possible fault, such as a broken P-lead, leaving a magneto “hot” and live even when switched off
questions.explain: No drop suggests the magneto isn’t being grounded. A “hot” magneto could fire the engine if the propeller is moved. Get it checked.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Why are fuel-injected engines less prone to induction icing than carbureted engines?
options: There’s no carburetor venturi where fuel vaporization cools the air
questions.explain: Ice forms in a carburetor because of fuel vaporization and pressure drop in the venturi, which a fuel-injected engine doesn’t have.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: You apply carburetor heat while ice is present. What does the RPM usually do?
options: Drops, then rises as the ice melts
questions.explain: Hot, less dense air first richens the mixture and drops RPM. As the ice melts, RPM rises.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: With a constant-speed propeller, what does the throttle control?
questions.explain: The throttle sets manifold pressure, and the propeller control sets RPM.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: With a constant-speed propeller, why avoid high manifold pressure at low RPM?
options: It can overstress the engine and cause detonation
It cools the engine too much
questions.explain: High manifold pressure with low RPM puts excessive pressure in the cylinders. When increasing power, increase RPM first; when reducing, reduce manifold pressure first.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: After engine start, how soon should the oil pressure show in the green?
options: Within about 30 seconds (longer in very cold weather)
questions.explain: Most POHs say oil pressure should rise within about 30 seconds. If not, shut the engine down.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: If the correct grade of avgas isn’t available, what should you do?
options: Use the next higher approved grade, never a lower one
questions.explain: A lower grade can cause detonation. Use only approved grades, preferring a higher one if the right grade isn’t available.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: What is preignition?
options: The spark firing at the right time
The mixture igniting before the normal spark, often from a hot spot in the cylinder
questions.explain: Preignition is uncontrolled ignition from hot spots before the spark plug fires. Detonation is explosive burning after it fires.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Why turn on pitot heat?
options: To stop ice from blocking the pitot tube in visible moisture near freezing
To clear fog from the windshield
questions.explain: Pitot heat prevents ice from blocking the pitot tube, which would make the airspeed indicator unreliable.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: Lines of latitude…
options: Run north–south and measure east–west position
Run east–west and measure position north or south of the equator
questions.explain: Latitude lines (parallels) run east–west. Meridians of longitude run north–south and meet at the poles.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: It’s 1500 Eastern Daylight Time. What time is it in UTC?
questions.explain: Eastern Daylight Time is UTC−4, so add 4 hours: 1900Z. Eastern Standard Time is UTC−5.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: What is the correct order for working out compass heading from true course?
options: True course → magnetic course → compass heading → true heading
True course ± wind correction = true heading ± variation = magnetic heading ± deviation = compass heading
questions.explain: Correct for wind first, then variation, then deviation. A common memory aid is TC → TH → MH → CH.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: True course is 180°, wind correction is 10° right, and variation is 7°W. What is the magnetic heading?
questions.explain: True heading = 180 + 10 = 190°. West variation is added (“west is best”): 190 + 7 = 197°.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: True course is 090°, wind from 360° at 20 knots, TAS 100 knots. Which way and roughly how much should you correct?
