questions.explain: The wind is from your left, so correct left. 20 ÷ 100 ≈ 0.2, and sin⁻¹ 0.2 ≈ 11.5°.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: On a VOR, the CDI needle is at full-scale deflection. About how far off the selected course are you?
questions.explain: Full scale on a VOR CDI is 10°, so each of the five dots is about 2°.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: The OBS is set to 180° with a TO indication and the needle centered. Where are you?
options: South of the station, on the 180° radial
North of the station, on the 360° radial
questions.explain: A TO flag on 180° means flying 180° takes you to the station, so you’re north of it, on the 360° radial.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: When checking a VOR receiver against a VOT, what is the allowed error?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.171: ±4° on a VOT or ground checkpoint, ±6° on an airborne checkpoint, and 4° between two receivers in a dual check.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: How do you make sure you’re using the right VOR and that it’s working?
options: Identify its Morse code; no ident usually means it’s under maintenance
questions.explain: Always identify the station by its Morse code. If the ident is missing, the VOR may be unreliable.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: What is dead reckoning?
options: Navigating by computing headings, groundspeed and time from known wind and airspeed
questions.explain: Dead reckoning is calculation from heading, speed, wind and time. Pilotage is navigating by visual landmarks.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: You fly 32 NM between checkpoints in 15 minutes. What is your groundspeed?
questions.explain: 32 NM in a quarter of an hour = 32 × 4 = 128 knots.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: How many statute miles is one nautical mile?
questions.explain: One nautical mile is about 1.15 statute miles, or 1,852 meters.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: On a sectional chart (1:500,000), about how many nautical miles does one inch represent?
questions.explain: At 1:500,000, one inch is about 6.86 NM (7.89 SM). Terminal area charts are 1:250,000.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: What is the agonic line?
options: A line joining places of equal magnetic variation
The line where magnetic variation is zero
questions.explain: Isogonic lines join places with the same variation. On the agonic line, variation is zero.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: VFR cruising altitudes are chosen based on your…
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.159 bases VFR cruising altitudes on magnetic course, not heading.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: Where can you find details such as an airport’s runway lengths, fuel and frequencies?
questions.explain: The Chart Supplement lists airport data, frequencies, services and remarks for each airport.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: How often are VFR sectional charts updated?
questions.explain: The FAA publishes sectionals on a 56-day cycle. Always fly with a current chart.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: As you climb at the same indicated airspeed, what happens to true airspeed?
options: It increases, by roughly 2% per 1,000 ft
questions.explain: Thinner air means a higher true airspeed for the same indicated airspeed, about 2% more per 1,000 ft.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes which type of hypoxia?
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin so blood can’t carry enough oxygen: hypemic hypoxia. Hypoxic hypoxia comes from altitude.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: How should you treat hyperventilation?
options: Slow your breathing rate, for example by talking aloud or breathing into a bag
Use supplemental oxygen at full flow only
questions.explain: Slowing your breathing lets carbon dioxide build back to normal. Talking aloud helps.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: What is the “graveyard spiral”?
options: After a long descending turn, the pilot feels level and pulls back, tightening the spiral and losing altitude fast
questions.explain: In a prolonged coordinated turn the inner ear stops sensing it. Seeing altitude drop, the pilot pulls back, tightening the spiral. Trust the instruments.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Which illusion comes from an abrupt head movement during a prolonged turn, and can be overwhelming?
questions.explain: Moving your head during a long turn stimulates other semicircular canals, giving a strong tumbling sensation.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: An abrupt change from a climb to straight-and-level flight can make you feel you’re tumbling backward. What is this?
questions.explain: The inversion illusion can make a pilot push the nose down abruptly, worsening the problem.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: A sloping cloud bank can make you bank the airplane to line up with it. What is this?
questions.explain: False horizons, such as sloping clouds or ground lights at night, can lead you to fly out of level.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: A runway that’s narrower than usual can make you think you’re…
options: Lower than you are, so you fly a high approach
Higher than you are, so you fly a low approach
questions.explain: A narrow runway looks like you’re higher than you are, so pilots tend to fly lower approaches.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: An upsloping runway can make you think you’re…
options: Higher than you are, so you fly too low
questions.explain: Upsloping runways look like you’re higher, which can lead to a dangerously low approach.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Approaching at night over water or unlit terrain toward a lit runway (a “black hole” approach), pilots tend to…
questions.explain: With no surrounding visual cues, pilots often perceive themselves as higher and fly a low approach. Use a VASI/PAPI or a stabilized glide path.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: To see a dim object at night, where should you look?
options: Slightly to one side of it (off-center viewing)
Close your eyes for a moment
questions.explain: The rods in your peripheral vision are more sensitive in the dark, so look 5° to 10° to one side of the object.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Why can night vision suffer above about 5,000 ft without supplemental oxygen?
options: Lower oxygen reduces the eye’s sensitivity in the dark
questions.explain: The eye’s rods are very sensitive to reduced oxygen, so night vision degrades well before other hypoxia symptoms.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: At night, a stationary light you stare at seems to move. What is this?
questions.explain: Autokinesis makes a fixed light appear to move after you’ve stared at it for several seconds. Keep your eyes moving.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: What is the antidote for the “anti-authority” hazardous attitude?
options: “Follow the rules, they are usually right”
questions.explain: Anti-authority (“don’t tell me”): follow the rules. Impulsivity: not so fast. Invulnerability: it could happen to me. Macho: taking chances is foolish. Resignation: I’m not helpless.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: A pilot thinks “it won’t happen to me”. Which hazardous attitude is this?
questions.explain: Invulnerability. The antidote is “it could happen to me”.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: A pilot facing a problem thinks “what’s the use, there’s nothing I can do”. Which hazardous attitude is this?
questions.explain: Resignation. The antidote is “I’m not helpless, I can make a difference”.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: In the PAVE risk checklist, what does each letter stand for?
questions.explain: PAVE is used to identify risk factors before a flight.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: What is the DECIDE model used for?
options: Making decisions systematically: Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate
questions.explain: DECIDE is a structured decision-making model from the FAA’s ADM guidance.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: A passenger feels airsick. What helps?
options: Opening the fresh air vents, looking outside at the horizon, and keeping maneuvers gentle
questions.explain: Fresh air, a view of the horizon and smooth flying reduce motion sickness.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Why should you avoid flying with a bad cold?
options: You might sneeze on the controls
Congestion can stop your ears and sinuses equalizing pressure, causing severe pain, especially in descent
questions.explain: Blocked Eustachian tubes or sinuses can’t equalize during descent, causing pain and even ear damage.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: What are personal minimums?
options: Your own limits for weather, conditions and experience, set before you fly and usually stricter than the legal minimums
questions.explain: Setting personal minimums before a flight takes the pressure out of go/no-go decisions in the moment.
